You have 1000 words. The phrase hangs in the air like a door held open by a single hinge, and I am already stepping through. It is a gift and a fence, a swimming pool with a shallow end and a deep end, and I have chosen to wade in without checking the temperature. What comes first? The sound of the keyboard, that mechanical heartbeat under my fingers, and the strange intimacy of knowing that every keystroke is both a declaration and a disappearance, a mark that stays and a thought that leaves.

The word “whatever” is a kind of surrender, a white flag raised not in defeat but in invitation. So here I go. I think of the number one thousand. It is round in a way that feels almost magical—ten hundred, a millennium in miniature, the length of a short story, the patience of a long conversation. I have this, and I must spend it wisely, or perhaps foolishly, which is the same thing when you are spending imagination. The clock is not ticking loudly; it is more like a quiet accumulation, sand in a glass that I cannot see but I feel the weight of, grain by grain, as it fills.

The first thing that comes is the color blue—not sky blue, not ocean blue, but the blue of a screen after midnight, when the pixels have turned tired and the light has become a kind of memory of itself. I think of rooms I have never been in, rooms that exist only because I have described them once in a dream I will not wake from. There is a chair in one of them, velvet, slightly worn at the elbow, and it smells of cedar and something else, something like the past. I have never owned a chair like that, but now I do, in this text, because words are the only real estate that belongs to everyone and no one at once, a shared hallucination we agree to call literature.

Then comes sound. Not music, exactly, but the texture of sound: the way rain hits a window that is already open to the weather, not protected by glass but merely framed by it, as if the window were a hesitation rather than a barrier. I remember a train station where the announcements were in a language I almost understood, and the crowd moved like a single organism, each person a cell, and I was the foreign body, the antigen, the interesting mistake. I stood still while they flowed around me, and that stillness felt like a victory. Now I feel it again, writing this, still at the center of a flow I cannot control, suspended in the current of my own making.

What else comes? The taste of copper, which is the taste of anticipation, of a coin waiting to be flipped, of blood that is not yet scared. I think of coins, of all the currency that has changed hands for stories, for lies told as truths, for truths told as jokes, for the silence that buys nothing and sells everything. I think of the economics of attention, which is the only economy that matters now, and how this very paragraph is a bid for yours, a small investment in a compound I am inventing as I speak, a speculative stock of consciousness.

There is a bird outside, or perhaps there is only the idea of a bird, and it is singing in a key that does not exist on a piano. It is singing about the distance between two points, and how that distance is not a straight line but a story, curved by the gravity of everything we have forgotten. I want to write about forgetting, because it is the shadow that makes memory visible. Without forgetting, the past would be a solid wall; with it, the past is a window with curtains that move when I am not looking, always in motion, always slightly wrong in my perception of them.

I think of hands. My hands, which are not actually in this room in any literal sense, but they are here in the architecture of the sentence, arranging and rearranging themselves like dancers who have forgotten the choreography but remember the feeling. The word “fingers” appears in my mind, and then “fingertips,” and then the strange intimacy of touching something cold—metal, marble, the edge of a page that has been turned too many times. There is a ritual to this, a ceremony of making the invisible visible, of turning thought into text, which is a kind of alchemy that never quite works but always almost does, a near-miss that is sweeter than success.

The number 1000 begins to feel like a horizon. I am walking toward it, or perhaps the horizon is walking toward me, and the distance between us is measured in syllables, in the small muscles of my mouth that are not moving but are simulated in the mind of the reader. Each word is a step. Some steps are long, some are short, some stumble over the root of an idea that has grown underground. I stumble now. I think of stumbles, of the poetry of error. A typo is a ghost in the machine, a visitor from another timeline where I chose a different word, a better word, a worse word, and I welcome it. I want the text to be imperfect because perfection is a prison with very comfortable walls, and I was never good at staying in comfortable places.

I drift to a memory of water—not rain this time, but a lake, still and dark, reflecting a sky that was either dawn or dusk, and in the reflection the trees were upside-down, and the world seemed more honest that way, inverted, truthful in its inversion. I wanted to jump in, not to swim but to dissolve, to become part of the surface tension, to lose the boundary between the observer and the observed. Writing is like that: you want to dissolve into the subject, to become the thing you are describing. But the boundary is what makes the observation possible, so I stay on the shore, waving at my own reflection, which is waving back with a delay.

Now I think of limits, because the user gave me one, and limits are interesting. A canvas has edges, a song has an ending, a life has a death, and a word count has a ceiling that is both arbitrary and absolute. But inside the limit, everything is possible. The sky inside a frame is not less sky; it is sky selected, sky curated by the act of looking. I am curating this sky now, and it is a strange sky, made of associations, half-thoughts, the occasional bright flash of clarity that comes like sunlight through cloud, brief and undeniable.

What is clarity? It is the moment when a sentence stops being about itself and becomes about something larger, a doorway that opens onto a room you did not know was there. I try to make that moment now. This sentence is about the feeling of reaching for something just out of hand, the way a child reaches for a star and then realizes that the star was never the point, only the reaching, only the posture of desire. I am reaching. I am not sure for what. Perhaps for the end of this paragraph, which is the small death of a thought, the surrender of its potential into the fixed form of punctuation.

I think of punctuation as breath. The comma is a small inhale, the period is a release, the semicolon is a hesitation, a moment of indecision that is itself a kind of decision, a choice to continue rather than conclude. I use them all, like a musician using dynamics, and I want the rhythm to vary, to not be monotonous, because life is not monotonous, even when it feels that way, especially when it feels that way. The rhythm of this writing is irregular, which is honest, which is the best I can offer.

Now, a shift. Let us talk about light, because light is the original writer, the first thing that made vision possible, and vision made language, and language made the world we live in. I imagine a room with one window, and the sun enters at a specific angle, cutting a rectangle on the floor that moves like a slow clock, measuring time not in seconds but in warmth. I have sat in such rooms, not in this life but in the life of ideas, and I have watched the light change, and I have understood that time is not a line but a texture, something you can feel against your skin, something that can make you feel alone or accompanied depending on the quality of the glow.

The word “texture” brings me back to the physical, to the substrate of reality. I think of fabrics, of wool and silk and the roughness of linen that has been washed too many times, and I think of clothing as language, as a way of saying “I belong” or “I do not belong” before the mouth has a chance to speak. I think of identity as a garment that we put on and take off, sometimes by accident, sometimes by design, and sometimes by the invisible pressure of the culture that sells us the idea that we are something specific, something branded.

There is a conversation happening somewhere, or not happening, which is the same thing when you think about it, because conversation is a fiction we agree to perform, a dance of nodding and interrupting that conceals more than it reveals. I imagine two people whose dialogue I have never heard but have invented entirely, and they are talking about the weather, but it is not the weather they mean, it is the gap between them, the silence that carries more weight than any word, the unspoken accusation that lives in the space between sentences.

But I must keep going. The word count is a river, and I am the boat, and I must keep paddling or I will become stagnant, and stagnation is the enemy of the living word, the thing that turns prose into stone. I think of movement, of walking, of the way a body moves through space, leaving a temporary impression, like a footprint in snow that melts before anyone can claim it, before anyone can say, “This was here.” Each word I write is a footprint, and the snow is your attention, which is melting fast, which is exactly why I must continue without apology, without too much self-awareness, though some self-awareness is necessary to avoid total chaos, to avoid becoming pure noise.

I think of chaos, and how it is not the opposite of order but its precondition. Before the universe was a clock, it was a cloud. Before I had a thought, I had noise, a static of possibility. This text is a cloud that is trying to become a clock, a noise that is trying to become music. It may not fully succeed, but the attempt is the art, the desire is the content, and the failure is a kind of success because it proves I was trying, I was alive to the attempt.

Now I think of endings, because everything ends, and this must end too, not because I am tired but because the container demands its closure. I think of the feeling of finishing something, the small satisfaction of a door closing, a light switching off, a breath held and then released into the common air. I want to end not with a bang but with a settling, with the feeling of dust returning to air, of the screen going black but the ideas remaining, faint, like stars in daylight that are still there if you know where to look, if you know that the sky is always full of light, always bright, always writing its own invisible poem.

So here is the end, or near it. I have used many of the words, not all, but enough to feel the shape of the limitation, the beautiful, arbitrary shape of a thousand, the curve of the container. I have written what came to me, which was everything and nothing, which was the color of a screen and the sound of a bird and the memory of a lake turned upside down. I have given you a journey that was not a straight line but a spiral, and spirals are good because they allow you to return to the center, to the self, to the simple fact of being here, writing, in this moment, with this many words remaining, until there are none, until the reservoir is empty and the vessel is full of air.

The last word is not important, but it is necessary. It is like the final dot of an i, the seal on a letter, the closing of an eye at sleep, the small exhale that says, “I have done what I could.” I write it now, and then I stop, and the space after it is not empty but full of everything I could not say, which is always the larger part, the shadow of the text, the true text that lives in the mind of the reader, where it has been rewritten, remembered, and made your own. Goodbye, reader, not because I leave, but because I have reached the edge of what this particular container can hold. What comes next is up to you. The words are yours now, as they always were, and they will continue in the silence where language begins again.
